source: Lieder and Griffiths (2020) Resource-rational analysis, BBS 43:e1
finding: Defines resource-rational analysis: derive the best cognitive strategy given the task, the environment and the brain's limits, then test it. Claims it joins rational models with realistic constraints.
numbers: Target article plus commentaries and authors' replies; no single N.
quote: measuring cognitive constraints remains challenging and often requires additional assumptions
limits: Authors admit that measuring cognitive constraints is hard, so models can be hard to falsify in practice.
agent_relevance: Gives the formal base for an S0 gate: spend thinking only while expected gain beats its cost.

source: Lieder and Griffiths (2020) Resource-rational analysis, BBS 43:e1 (reporting Callaway et al. planning work)
finding: In a planning task, people reached about 86% of the best possible trade-off between decision quality and time cost. They matched the bounded-optimal strategy only about 55% of the time.
numbers: 86% of optimal trade-off; 55% strategy agreement.
limits: Second-hand in this line; the primary paper (Callaway et al. 2022, Nature Hum Behav) was paywalled and not opened.
agent_relevance: People are near but not at the optimum. A rule-based gate need not be perfect to beat unaided intuition.

source: Lieder and Griffiths (2020) Resource-rational analysis, BBS 43:e1 (reporting Vul et al. 2014)
finding: Optimal number of mental samples per decision is very small. One sample (probability matching) is bounded-optimal when acting takes at most 3 times as long as simulating. More samples pay off as stakes rise.
numbers: Threshold ratio 3:1 (execution time to simulation time). Incentive studies cited: Shanks 2002, Vulkan 2000.
limits: Second-hand; Vul et al. not opened. Qualitative fit to incentive studies only.
agent_relevance: Stakes and action cost should set the sample count in S0, not a fixed N.

source: Lieder and Griffiths (2020) Resource-rational analysis, BBS 43:e1 (reporting Lieder et al. 2018 anchoring)
finding: Anchoring was reread as a rational choice of how many adjustments to make from an initial guess. Old view: people think too little.
numbers: Model: adjustments follow the speed-accuracy trade-off (their Eq. 3).
limits: Second-hand; the 2018 paper hit a cookie wall and was not opened. Rival view that anchoring is plain error is not tested here.
agent_relevance: A competing explanation for 'too little thinking' results: the stop was cost-sensitive.

source: Lieder and Griffiths (2020) Resource-rational analysis, BBS 43:e1 (reporting resource-rational heuristic discovery)
finding: Automatic derivation of bounded-optimal heuristics found a new strategy mixing satisficing and Take-The-Best (SAT-TTB). A follow-up experiment found people use it in the environments where it is bounded-optimal.
numbers: One discovered heuristic; one confirming experiment (N not read).
limits: Second-hand; single lab.
agent_relevance: Heuristics can be matched to environment type; supports a stop rule that depends on task type.

source: Beck et al. (2012) as discussed in BBS target article
finding: Rival claim: measured neural noise is too small to explain human suboptimality, so the brain may use approximations with systematic bias instead. Authors answer that approximations are bounded-optimal under complexity limits.
numbers: No numbers given in the discussion.
limits: A debate point, not a test. Not decided by data in the paper.
agent_relevance: Warns that 'limited resources' may be a post-hoc label for any error.

source: Commentary and reply in BBS 43 (degrees of freedom, file drawer)
finding: Critics say adding costs and capacities adds free parameters and risks just-so stories. Authors say the constraints can be measured independently and models should be judged by prediction of phenomena they were not built for. They concede a publication bias is plausible but say they have seen no evidence of it.
numbers: No replication count exists; authors state RRA adds 2 degrees of freedom (computational resources and their costs).
quote: guard against this, one should ideally base all assumptions about the constraints on independent empirical measurements
limits: No systematic failed-replication record found. The file-drawer concern is open.
agent_relevance: Treat any fitted cost parameter as a guess [D] until tested on held-out tasks (G3).

source: Lieder and Griffiths (2020) Resource-rational analysis, BBS 43:e1 (section 6, challenges)
finding: Boundary conditions: hard to apply during adaptation to a new environment, for rare situations with low stakes, and when the environment or constraints are unknown.
numbers: Qualitative list.
limits: Authors' own statement of limits.
agent_relevance: S0 gate is least reliable on novel task types: use a conservative default budget there.

source: Lieder and Griffiths (2020) Resource-rational analysis, BBS 43:e1 (reporting Gabaix and Laibson)
finding: A myopic cost-benefit rule (pick the next computation by immediate expected gain minus cost) predicted people's suboptimal search in a simple bandit task and multi-attribute choice better than earlier models.
numbers: Gabaix et al. 2006; numbers not given in the review.
limits: Second-hand. Myopic rules ignore later computations.
agent_relevance: Supports a cheap one-step value-of-computation check in code.

source: Lieder, Shenhav, Musslick, Griffiths (2018) Rational metareasoning and the plasticity of cognitive control, PLOS Comput Biol
finding: LVOC model: people learn by reinforcement the value of control signals, using stimulus features. It predicted learning and transfer in one visual attention experiment and four Stroop/Flanker experiments, and beat two rivals.
numbers: 5 experiments. Rescorla-Wagner model MSE 3.33 vs LVOC 1.35 (one experiment, same parameter count). Win-Stay Lose-Shift failed to show gradual improvement.
limits: Only two rival models compared. Fits are model-to-data, not preregistered tests.
agent_relevance: Learned value of effort can be trained from outcomes, a hint for tuning the gate from logs.

source: Callaway, Gul, Krueger, Griffiths, Lieder (2017) Learning to select computations
finding: BMPS approximates the optimal choice of computations. In simulated environments it reached 98.4% of optimal (trees of height 2 and 3) and 99.1% in a Bernoulli metalevel task, and beat a meta-greedy policy.
numbers: 98.4% and 99.1% of optimal; beat meta-greedy by 6.78 to 35.8% where optimal made more than one observation (p<0.0001).
limits: Simulation only, small problems where the optimum can be computed. No human or LLM data.
agent_relevance: Shows a near-optimal stop/continue rule is learnable; basis for a coded S0 policy.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, Griffiths (2024/2025) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models
finding: A reward based on value of computation (utility of chain of thought minus a per-token cost) was used to train Llama models. They used fewer reasoning tokens at equal or better accuracy than STaR.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B: accuracy 63.5% vs STaR 61.9%, output tokens 146.2 vs 215.1. Llama-3.2-3B: 50.1% vs 47.4%, 170.8 vs 222.7 tokens. 23-32% fewer tokens than STaR; 35-42% fewer than few-shot CoT. Cost weight 0.1, 4096 training samples.
limits: Needs fine-tuning. Two small base models. Datasets include ARC, GSM8K, ProofWriter.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM test of the Lieder-Griffiths idea; shows the cost term works as an effort dial.

source: De Sabbata et al. (2024/2025) adaptive length split
finding: Models spent fewer tokens on easy than hard items. Instruct CoT did not adapt at all. RaM widened the gap.
numbers: Easy vs hard tokens, 3B: RaM 72 vs 145 (50.3% reduction); STaR 128 vs 195; CoT instruct 221 vs 222 (0.5%). 8B: RaM 89 vs 139 (36.0%).
limits: Easy defined as items direct few-shot already solved.
agent_relevance: Instruction-tuned models do not scale thinking to difficulty by themselves; a coded gate should.

source: De Sabbata et al. (2024/2025) out-of-distribution test
finding: On MMLU-CF, RaM used 28-36% fewer tokens than STaR. Accuracy gain did not hold in one case.
numbers: 3B: 29.5% vs 27.0%. 8B: 36.4% vs 40.2% (3.8 points worse than STaR). Subjects needing multi-step reasoning showed smaller cuts.
limits: Cost saving can cost accuracy out of distribution.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: a cost term trained in-domain can under-think elsewhere.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=?
finding: o1-like models overthink easy items. For 'what is 2 plus 3' they used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models and wrote 13 solutions.
numbers: In over 92% of correct cases the first solution round was already correct. First round was under 60% of tokens (QwQ on ASDIV: 287 tokens, 38.7%). More solutions on easier sets.
limits: Math sets; QwQ-32B-Preview and DeepSeek-R1 only.
agent_relevance: Strong case for an S0 gate: extra rounds on easy items add cost, not accuracy.

source: Chen et al. (2024) mitigation by self-training
finding: Training on shortened answers cut tokens while keeping accuracy. Keeping the first correct solution plus one reflection did best.
numbers: 48.6% fewer tokens at the same MATH500 accuracy (QwQ-32B-Preview). First-correct-solution only lost accuracy on hard MATH500; adding reflection beat it by 1.4%.
limits: Hard items still need reflection; pure truncation hurts.
agent_relevance: Stop after first verified answer, but keep one check on hard items.

source: Aggarwal and Welleck (2025) L1: Controlling How Long A Reasoning Model Thinks, COLM
finding: RL on length constraints gives a 1.5B model whose accuracy rises smoothly with the token budget in the prompt. It beat S1 length control.
numbers: Up to 100% relative and 20% absolute over S1; short-reasoning models gained up to 10% at equal length; a 1.5B model matched GPT-4o at the same token budget.
limits: 1.5B base only (R1-distilled). Needs RL training.
agent_relevance: Accuracy-versus-budget curve is smooth, so a budget dial is a valid control knob.

source: Aggarwal and Welleck (2025) L1-Max versus L1-Exact
finding: An exact budget wastes tokens on easy items. A max budget lets the model stop early and still respects the ceiling.
numbers: L1-Max often used up to 2x fewer tokens than L1-Exact at equal accuracy.
limits: Shown on math sets.
agent_relevance: Use a ceiling plus early stop, not a fixed budget.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally
finding: Best use of test-time compute depends on prompt difficulty. Allocating per prompt beat best-of-N with about 4x less compute. For questions where a small model has non-trivial success, test-time compute beat a 14x larger model in a FLOPs-matched test.
numbers: 4x efficiency gain; 14x model size; difficulty in five levels from base-model pass rates.
limits: On the hardest questions test-time compute gave very little benefit. MATH, PaLM-2 variants.
agent_relevance: Matches the value-of-computation view: allocate by estimated difficulty, and skip hopeless items.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: 1,000 curated examples plus budget forcing (append 'Wait' to extend thinking, force an end to cut it) gave controllable scaling.
numbers: AIME24 rose from 50% to 57% with extra thinking; beat o1-preview by up to 27% on MATH and AIME24.
limits: Gains flatten at long lengths; one 32B model. Forced stop is cruder than a value rule.
agent_relevance: Shows more thinking can be bought on demand, so the gate has something to switch.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute, TMLR
finding: Longer reasoning can lower accuracy. Five failure modes: Claude distracted by irrelevant data, o-series overfit to framing, drift to spurious features, lost focus on deduction, more self-preservation talk.
numbers: Tasks: counting with distractors, regression with spurious features, Zebra puzzles, AI-risk probes; accuracy falls as reasoning length rises (Claude Opus 4 on Misleading Math, e.g.).
limits: Constructed tasks, not a natural mix.
agent_relevance: Hard boundary for any rule that says 'more thinking is never worse'; supports a cap and G1.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AdaptThink
finding: RL teaches the model to pick Thinking or NoThinking by difficulty. Cuts length and raises accuracy.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: length -53% and accuracy +2.4% on average; GSM8K -50.9% / +4.1%; MATH500 -63.5% / +1.4%; AIME24 -44.7% / +1.6%.
limits: Small 1.5B model; math only.
agent_relevance: Skipping thinking is right on easy items: an S0 'no scaffold' path is justified.

source: Fang, Ma, Wang (2025) Thinkless: LLM Learns When to Think
finding: A trained model decides between short and long chain of thought by task complexity and its own ability.
numbers: Reduces long-chain use by 50% to 90% (abstract, incl. GSM8K).
limits: Only the abstract and setup were read; accuracy per set not recorded.
agent_relevance: Second independent system that learns the when-to-think decision.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Know When They're Right
finding: A probe on hidden states predicts whether an intermediate answer is correct, and was used to exit reasoning early.
numbers: 24% fewer tokens with accuracy 88.2% vs 88.2% no early exit (threshold set by grid search); a 0.9 threshold gave 88.6% equal to no-exit.
limits: Open-weights models; needs hidden-state access.
agent_relevance: A learned stop signal is a stand-in for the value of computation. With API-only models we need check-based signals.

source: Liu, Zhang, Griffiths et al. (2025) Large Language Models Assume People are More Rational than We Really Are, ICLR
finding: LLMs predict human risky choices as more rational than people are. Spearman correlation with expected value: 0.94 for the LLM, 0.48 for humans.
numbers: choices13k, 13,006 problems. GPT-4o CoT simulation 0.90 with expected value. Best LLM-to-human match: GPT-4-Turbo r=0.60, MSE 0.13.
limits: Abstract gambles only.
agent_relevance: Do not use an LLM as a model of how much effort real users spend; CoT pushes toward the rational answer.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Turning large language models into cognitive models
finding: A fine-tuned LLM (CENTaUR) matched human regret in a bandit task and a horizon task, but LLaMA alone did not.
numbers: Bandit regret: humans 1.24, CENTaUR 1.35, LLaMA 1.85. Horizon: humans 2.33, CENTaUR 2.38, LLaMA 7.21.
limits: Needs fine-tuning on human data.
agent_relevance: Raw LLMs are poor explorers; this is a boundary for explore/stop choices.

source: Lieder and Griffiths (2020) reply: competing 'think too little' view
finding: Older heuristics-and-biases view: people usually think too little. RRA view: apparent underthinking can be the optimal stop under cost.
numbers: No decisive discriminating experiment is reported in the paper beyond the anchoring and sampling cases above.
limits: Rival accounts can fit the same data. Discriminating tests are rare.
agent_relevance: Do not claim an LLM overthinks or underthinks without a measured cost per token.
